summary.title: How I Find Problems to Solve as a Staff Engineer
summary.one_liner: Learn a personal method for turning everyday engineering complaints and requests into high-impact project ideas by listening broadly, letting problems accumulate, and pressure-testing them before building.
keywords: how do you find problems worth working on
stewardship and trust in engineering orgs
takeaways: Listen to day-to-day problems and requests, then dig past the requested solution to the underlying need.
Let potential problems accumulate instead of acting on the first request, since urgency is not the same as importance.
Look for common shapes across seemingly unrelated requests, but treat a neat pattern as a hypothesis to test.
Pressure-test ideas with prototypes, RFCs and feedback before committing large effort, and be willing to stop or park them.
Solving useful problems builds trust and brings you into more conversations, which surfaces the next problems.
summary.summary: A personal essay by a Staff Engineer (Lalit Maganti) describing how he identifies problems worth solving, mainly in infrastructure and developer tools at large companies with bottom-up autonomy. He describes listening to the stream of team pain points, probing for root issues behind requests, seeking out people with cross-organization visibility, and deliberately delaying action so evidence can accumulate. The main worked example is Perfetto, where many small feature requests revealed a common need to extend the UI, leading to macros and extension servers. The post also covers the risks of acting too fast, the caching-system idea that turned out to need two separate solutions, and how solved problems build trust over time.
